A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same research work. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including the material moved from v1 Appendices D-F to v2 Appendices F-H.

before.justification: V1 reports original simulation results, ablations, and failure analyses in Figures 4-7, plus real-robot results from 20 trials per task.

after.justification: V2 retains the original empirical evaluations and adds baseline comparisons, VLM evaluations, and noise experiments in Table 6 and Figures 9-11.

M1.justification: The described procedure adds VLM elicitation of keypoint names before coordinate localization, using a standardized prompt in Section 3.2 and Appendix H.1. V1 starts with task-specific named-keypoint prompts. Trajectory interpolation, residual PPO, rewards, and the termination curriculum remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The eight simulated and three physical tasks remain. V2 adds deliberately corrupted-waypoint scenarios and revises stated task requirements: Move Bottle now requires upright placement, and physical hammering requires contact strikes rather than grasped swings. These are limited scenario changes, not a new benchmark suite.

E2.justification: V2 adds IKER to Figure 4, simple- and complex-reward RL baselines to Figure 9, and Diffusion Policy with 10, 20, and 50 demonstrations to Figure 10. Table 6 additionally compares Molmo with Gemini. These substantially broaden v1's comparisons with oracles and pre-recorded trajectories.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include matched oracle-keypoint RL controls, demonstration-budget comparisons, separate VLM keypoint/trajectory assessments, and Gaussian waypoint noise during training and inference. Appendix C.3 also changes physical hammer initialization and success criteria to a table-resting hammer and three observable contact strikes. These reported protocol revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds waypoint-noise sensitivity tests on Apple, Drawer, Hammer, and Scissors, a demonstration-count sweep for Diffusion Policy, and component-level diagnosis of Molmo's keypoint versus trajectory performance. These extend the retained iterative-refinement, waypoint-count, oracle-component, and failure-decomposition analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions report policy results across three seeds with standard errors; Figures 9-11 extend that existing practice. The physical evaluation remains 20 trials across four plans per task. No new confidence intervals, significance tests, or explicit increase in replication is reported.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive baseline and robustness results, including IKER's 32% mean success and Molmo's 100% keypoint correctness but 0% feasible trajectories on all three tested tasks. Figure 4 changes pre-recorded Apple success from 18% to 13% and its overall mean from 20% to 19%. Proposed-method means remain 72% zero-shot and 81% few-shot, although new prose mislabels 72% as few-shot. Figure 9 also reports 82% for Drawer with oracle keypoints, while Figure 7 retains 62%, without explaining the difference.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation, objectives, Equations 1-5, and damped inverse-kinematics derivation are retained. V2 introduces no substantive theoretical revision, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and main conclusion retain the contribution of VLM-generated scaffolds combined with residual RL for dexterous manipulation without human demonstrations or handcrafted task rewards, including sim-to-real transfer. Added comparisons do not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands applicability qualifications beyond rigidity, planner-controller feedback, and latency. It discusses orientation limitations with few keypoints, possible force/torque signals, generalization to new tasks or object categories, and precision-sensitive sim-to-real transfer. Appendices C.7 and D add reachability explanations and interpretations of Molmo's planning failures.

D1.justification: V2 supplies the keypoint-elicitation prompt, reachability and plan-sampling details, and implementation descriptions for added comparisons. Existing hyperparameter tables and hardware descriptions remain. The first-page resource notice changes from 'Videos and Code' to 'Videos'; the PDFs alone do not establish whether external code availability changed.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to Diffusion Policy, Molmo/Pixmo, object-oriented rewards, and Point Policy, and expands motion-tracking discussion to include behavior cloning. The central positioning against demonstration-dependent approaches remains unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 rewrites the real-world and limitations passages, incorporates simulation results into Section 4.1, and inserts new appendix sections while retaining the previous appendix material. The overall narrative remains recognizable. Front matter changes from a preprint notice to NeurIPS 2025.

P2.justification: V2 adds three multi-task figures covering RL comparisons, imitation-learning comparisons, and noise sensitivity, plus the VLM comparison table. Figure 4 gains an IKER series and legend entry. Existing diagrams and qualitative images are retained with local resizing and page-flow changes.

improvement.justification: The broader alternative-method comparisons, noise tests, and expanded limitations provide useful additional validation and clearer applicability boundaries. The net gain is limited by new reporting inconsistencies: the 72%/81% few-shot mismatch and unexplained 62%/82% Drawer oracle-keypoint results in Figures 7 and 9. Revised task requirements also lack an explicit connection to rerun evaluations.
